_comment: How every report section is CALCULATED, in one place.
Sections that look thin ('why is Easy misses only two rows?') or surprising
('why is the top spot a private yard?') are usually correct and just opaque.
This file is the answer, and it is shared so the answer cannot differ
between the Markdown report and the app:
- birding-app/www/section-docs.json  is the canonical copy (bundled, so
the in-app info button works with no network).
- birding/section-docs.json          is a vendored copy report.py reads
- birding/tests/parity/test_section_docs.py asserts the two files are
byte-identical AND that every section in report-contract.json has an
entry, so a new section cannot ship undocumented.
Keys are the 'at' ids in tests/fixtures/report-contract.json.
'inputs' names the feeds. 'how' is the ordered calculation. 'limits' is what
the section CANNOT tell you - the most useful half, and the half a reader
can never infer from the output.

surgeBtn.summary: Detects a crowd forming right now, rather than a bird merely being present.
inputs: county recent + notable feeds
the region's Top 100 board
hotspot activity in the same feeds
how: Four independent lanes run over feeds other sections already pay for, so this costs no extra fetching.

Celebrity Birds: species eBird flags as NOTABLE here that you still need, reported within your chase distance in the last 24 hours, one row per BIRD rather than per report - the same bird at three ponds is one decision, not three. Closest first. This lane leads: the other three are about what OTHER birders are doing.

Each row is ONE line - code, count, locations, observations, where, when - and every fact on it comes from the SAME report: the nearest one, which is the one the distance is measured to. A row taking its place from one sighting and its time from another would read as a single observation and not be one. The labelled Nearest/Latest rows this replaced spent three lines of card on four short facts.

NOTABLE, not merely unseen. Asked for as "happening now should be things local birders would talk about without having to check ebird" - and three people reporting a bird that is ordinary here is well corroborated and still nobody mentions it. A bird earns this lane by being unusual HERE, not by being missing from your year list, so an unseen-but-ordinary bird belongs in All unseen reports and Closest spots, which are the sections about you.

A thin report must ALSO be either reviewed by eBird or seen 3 times: a mega found an hour ago has exactly one report and is worth keeping, while a single UNREVIEWED report is the "one off that might not be real".
Places that read as private - a named residence, a street address, bare coordinates - are never offered as somewhere to drive, in this lane as in every other place-ranking section.

Observation surge: distinct OBSERVERS (not checklists — one birder filing three lists is how a quiet spot fakes a crowd) in the last 36 h, against that species' trailing baseline at that place, clustered to 300 m.

Leaderboard cascade: 3+ of the region's top 100 adding the same species within 3 days. Sees counties our feeds never cover, lags up to a day. The board names the bird and the date and nothing else, so the place and time on the row come from a species-scoped state feed - that is where to actually go. Same one-line format as Celebrity Birds; the roster and the other reports are behind the expander.

Hotspot convergence: species-blind. It fires when a place gets unusually busy even if no bird was ever flagged notable — which is how a locally-regular bird draws twenty birders without tripping a rarity alert.
A surge needs two distinct observers AND two distinct checklists. Two names on one shared checklist is one observation, not corroboration.
limits: The nearby-needs lane is deliberately SHORT: 24 hours and your chase distance. A bird you need that has been around for a week is still worth having, and it is in All unseen reports - the point of an alert is that it is short enough to read.
A report whose date cannot be read is dropped from that lane rather than assumed fresh, because "just now" is the only thing the lane claims.
The baseline is measured from the data actually fetched (7 days), capped at the configured window, so a short feed cannot inflate every ratio.
With no trailing history at all the row reads "new here" and prints no ratio — a ratio over a zero denominator invents precision.

wxBtn.summary: Whether today's weather and tide favour going out, for the region's home coordinate.
inputs: NOAA forecast (US only)
NOAA tides for the region's station
how: Sunrise, sunset and civil twilight are computed for the home coordinate, in the region's local time.

Tides are listed one row per WINDOW, not per turning point, because the fact that decides whether you leave the house is when the water is coming IN — reconstructing that from two adjacent turning points is work the reader should not do.
Rising windows are marked 👀: an incoming tide pushes waterfowl and shorebirds closer in.
The last window of the day runs past midnight and is kept — an overnight incoming tide is exactly when the good shorebird chases happen.
limits: Tides need a NOAA station id; inland regions leave it blank and get no tide table.

dueBackBtn.summary: Which birds are about to return to the region, from seven years of archived records.
how: Takes every species ever recorded in the region (eBird's region checklist) and asks GBIF when each one historically shows up.
Most of that is already answered: the arrival table is harvested once in the report repo and ships with the app, so the phone only asks about species the table does not cover.
A species present all year has no arrival to predict and is skipped; only genuine migrants get a date.
"Present all year" counts months carrying at least 1% of the species' records, not months with a single straggler in them - the difference moved 106 of 295 Washington migrants out of "resident".
The date is the first day of the season that reaches 5% of the peak day's records, pooled across every year GBIF holds - so it is the long-term pattern, not one unusual spring.
Shows anything due within 30 days, plus anything that arrived in the last 14, because a bird already back is the one you can act on today.
🔍 marks a bird you still need; the rest are ones you have already recorded this year.
inputs: The bundled arrival table (arrivals.js), harvested from GBIF once per state
eBird product/spplist for the region (the same cached species index the lookup uses - no extra eBird traffic)
GBIF occurrence/search month and day facets, for anything the table does not cover
limits: App-only: the report is built once from a fixed snapshot and committed, and 'what arrives in the next three weeks' is a question whose answer moves every day.
Only Washington is harvested so far. Any other region falls back to reading GBIF live, which takes a few minutes the first time; it can be stopped and resumes where it left off.
GBIF lags about a year, so this is the long-term pattern and never this season's actual birds - it says when to start looking, not that anything is here.
A species too sparse in the archive to give a stable date is left out rather than guessed at.
Arrival is measured for the whole state, not your chase radius: a bird can be back on the coast a week before it reaches you.
A winter bird whose peak is January is measured from December, so its date can read as the start of that window rather than its true arrival in autumn.

scoutBtn.summary: A temporary home: what is actually being reported around somewhere else.
how: Type a place - a town, a reserve, or a pasted "lat, lng" - and it is geocoded, then three calls are made against that point.
Recent and notable observations within 50 km (eBird's own cap on a geo feed), over the last 7 days.
Every eBird hotspot within the same 50 km, in ONE call - 246 of them around Yakima.
Birds you still need lead the list, closest first, one row per species with its nearest place. Distances are from the scouted point, not from home.
One slot: scouting somewhere new replaces it. It survives a relaunch, because three calls should not be spent twice on the same answer.
inputs: a geocoder (keyless) to turn typed text into a point
data/obs/geo/recent and .../notable around that point
ref/hotspot/geo for the hotspot list
limits: App-only: the report is built for one region from a fixed home and committed. "What is being reported around Yakima right now" is asked on the way out of the door, and the answer would be stale before a document reached you.

The place lookup uses a third-party geocoder this project does not control, and it has been unreachable on device before. If a name will not resolve, paste coordinates instead - "46.6021, -120.5059" - which are read on the phone and need no lookup at all.
Three calls, whatever the distance - measured, not estimated. The hotspot list is the cheapest part of it, which is the opposite of how it feels.
Scoped by RADIUS, not by county, because a temporary home should cover what a home covers. A county feed would be a wider net than the question asked for, and would need a region lookup first.
50 km is eBird's cap on a geo feed, so a place with its birding an hour further out will not show it.
It does NOT touch your own report: your seen list decides what counts as needed, and nothing here is written back to it.
Species feeds (one per unseen bird, ~25 more calls) are deliberately NOT fetched - this is a look, not a move.

rankBtn.summary: Your standing on the region's eBird Top 100, plus the board itself.
inputs: ebird.org/top100 for the region (public HTML, no API key)
how: The board is fetched for the report's primary region only — one report, one region, one board.
eBird's default top100 ordering is already by species, so no explicit sort is requested.
The page self-identifies its region in a canonical link; a board that does not match is rejected and refetched rather than rendered under the wrong heading.
"of N eBirders" comes from a separate endpoint that needs eBird's own web token, scraped from the site bundle.
limits: eBird runs a proof-of-work bot filter on some region pages. When the token cannot be resolved the field size is omitted rather than failing the section — so a missing "of N" means degraded, not zero.
Each published day is a dated snapshot; eBird cannot re-serve yesterday's board.

refreshBtn.summary: Every rare-bird checklist filed TODAY in the report's counties, one row per report.
inputs: /data/obs/{county}/recent/notable for each county
geo notable feed around home
how: Filtered to today's date in the region's local time, deduped by CHECKLIST so two observers reporting the same bird both stand.
Newest first, and every row carries the clock time — a rarity is chased within hours, so a bare date decides nothing.
One row per checklist, not per species: a bird found at six places is six places you could drive to.

The card gives the bird's name a row of its own. Everything else — whether you still need it (🔍), how many were seen, whether it has stayed put (📍 Day N), where, when and who — sits on the line beneath it, because the one thing you scan a rarity list for is WHICH BIRD.
Reports beyond the chase radius are collapsed into an expander rather than dropped: a bird you still need is worth a longer drive on the right day.
How rare each species is across the whole snapshot is deliberately NOT here — that is what 🚨 Last 7-Days rarity reports answers.
limits: "Notable" is eBird's own review flag for the region; a bird that is rare to YOU but common locally will not appear here.

activeBtn.summary: Every notable report in the last 7 days, not just today's.
inputs: the same county + geo notable feeds, over the full 7-day window
how: Grouped by species, then by location, most recent first.
A multi-day presence is marked, because a bird seen on three separate days is a stakeout you can plan around rather than a fly-by.
limits: This is the largest section in the report. Ten checklists at one pond is still one place to drive to; deduping it by location is open backlog work.

abaBtn.summary: ABA Code 3+ birds — continental-scale rarities, normally 0-3 of them.
inputs: the ABA Rarities needs alert (SN10489)
a rolling local archive of that alert
the region's own notable feed
how: Three complementary sources are UNIONED. The alert page caps at 500 observations continent-wide and is a shifting window, so a state bird can fall off it entirely; the archive supplies memory and the region feed supplies scope.
Species are kept only if the ABA checklist codes them 3 or higher.

Because these are strange birds you may never have seen, each gets a full card: a large photo, the name at headline size, a description, and the rarity evidence — how many reports, observers, distinct places and days it has, which for a Code 3+ bird is often a single digit. The app also counts reports ABA-wide and how many states or provinces have it at all, because it holds the unfiltered alert; the report is already state-scoped and shows the local numbers only.
limits: Review status changes; a record shown here may later be reclassified.

lastNewBtn.summary: Turns the leaderboard into a chase board: what the region's top birders just added.
inputs: the region's Top 100 board (each row prints that birder's most recent year tick)
how: The 'most recent addition' column is grouped BY SPECIES. When nine of the top hundred share the same newest bird, it is demonstrably findable now.
Sorted most-shared first, then freshest.
One board only — the region's own. Pooling a national board recommends birds you cannot drive to.
Each species expands to recent in-region checklists: five, or more if there are more inside the 3-day fresh window, capped so a bird everybody refinds cannot emit hundreds of links.
limits: The board updates roughly daily, so a tick can be up to a day old.

tripBtn.summary: A chained route of up to 4 stops that maximises NEW unseen birds per hop.
inputs: unseen reports from the last 7 days
how: An anchor hotspot must hold at least 2 unseen species.
Each additional stop must be within 15 mi of the previous one AND add at least 2 species new to the route, or 1 new rarity — otherwise the hop is not worth driving.
Up to 10 target birds are listed per stop, and the whole route links out as a Google Maps itinerary.
limits: Greedy, not optimal: it chains the best next hop rather than solving the whole route.

destBtn.summary: The places holding the most unseen birds, ranked by how many you would gain.
inputs: county recent + notable feeds
geo feeds around home
how: Reports are clustered to a single place, then scored on unseen species count with rarities weighted up.
Distance is measured from home, matching the report.
limits: Ranked by birds, not by drive time — the top row can be an hour away.

targetsBtn.summary: The nearest place holding a bird you still need.
inputs: /data/obs/{county}/recent for each county in the report
the notable feeds
the geo feeds around home
how: Start from every observation in the report's own county and geo feeds — this is county-scoped, not statewide.
Drop anything you have already seen this year, using the taxonomy parent chain so a subspecies of a bird you have seen does not read as unseen.
Apply the chaseability gate (see limits) — a bird you cannot legally go and look at is not a target.
Cluster what remains to 250 m so ten reports from one pond become one place.

Measure each cluster from home. There used to be a second fixed anchor, the workplace, so a spot by the office ranked on its short hop; it was retired because a stored workplace is a guess about where you will be, and the app's current-location anchor is not.
Keep one record per species per cluster (the most recent), sort rarities first, then sort the clusters closest-first.
Show everything within 30 mi, at least the 10 nearest, never more than 40.
limits: The chaseability gate rejects a location whose NAME says it is closed — a parenthesised 'private', 'restricted', 'no public access' and similar. That is checked before anything else, so even a well-attested stakeout at such a place is dropped.

A location eBird marks private is still shown when it qualifies as a stakeout: 3+ distinct checklists within 300 m, which is what a roadside viewing point outside someone's yard looks like in the data. That is why a residential address can legitimately appear.

THE BIG ONE: the per-county 'recent' feed returns exactly ONE observation per species. So a needed bird has at most a handful of known locations in the whole dataset, and the nearest of those may be far from the nearest place it actually is. This section is sparse by construction, not by accident.

quickBtn.summary: An impulse detour: the richest hotspots a few minutes from where you are.
inputs: ref/hotspot/geo around the chosen anchor
how: Pick the anchor — home, your current location, or a place you search for. Home is the default, which is what the Markdown report uses.
Hotspots are scored on all-time species with a distance decay, so a 40-species puddle two minutes away does not beat a real site.
But the LIST IS SORTED BY DISTANCE, not by score: score decides which spots make the cut, proximity decides the order.
The radius starts at 5 mi and widens to 10 then 15 rather than print an empty section in a sparse region.
Hotspots birded in the last 10 days are penalised but not removed.
limits: This is about places, not birds — it does not know what is being seen there today.
In the app the origin is yours to choose, so the rows can differ from the Markdown report, which can only ever rank from a fixed anchor.

excBtn.summary: Longer drives that are worth it — the best unseen-bird haul per mile.
inputs: the same clustered unseen reports as Top destinations
how: Scored on unseen species relative to drive distance, so a distant site has to earn its mileage.
limits: Uses straight-line distance, not road distance.

hotBtn.summary: Hotspots getting unusually busy in the last 30 days.
inputs: a bulk 30-day observation feed for the region
how: A hotspot qualifies on at least 5 fresh sightings inside the 30-day window.
Ranked on the surge relative to that hotspot's own normal activity, so a famously busy site does not permanently occupy the list.
Each row lists the birds actually being reported there with species counts and recent checklists.
limits: Bounded to about 35 mi from home by default.

coldBtn.summary: Good hotspots nobody is watching — where a find is yours to make.
inputs: hotspot reference data
a 30-day recent-activity probe per hotspot
historic samples from up to 3 previous years
how: A hotspot needs at least 100 all-time species to qualify — an overlooked gem has to be a gem first.
Scored on days of silence (with diminishing returns past 30) against its historic productivity for this time of year, sampled around the 5th, 15th and 25th of the month across up to 3 years.
A hotspot with no historic sample is reported as UNMEASURED, not as new: absence of a norm is not evidence of neglect.
limits: Bounded to about 35 mi from home by default.

cklBtn.summary: Recent checklists in your counties - ranked by species count (Birdiest), or newest first.
inputs: checklist feeds for public hotspots in the region
how: Last 7 days, public hotspots only, within 40 mi of home, best checklist per hotspot, top 25.
Birds you still need are flagged inside each checklist.

Two modes over ONE cached per-county product/lists feed, so the second costs no extra call: Birdiest keeps the best checklist per hotspot, Newest keeps every checklist in order. Birdiest is the default.
limits: One checklist per hotspot, so a site with two great lists appears once.

convoyBtn.summary: Groups of birders who moved between the same places together — a route you can copy.
inputs: checklists from the region's feeds, plus the taxonomy for species resolution
how: Birders filing checklists at the same places within a short window on the same day are detected as a convoy.
Every member's checklist at every stop is pooled. Two birders standing together file different lists, so reading only one drops birds the other wrote down.
Each convoy is titled with its date, party size, stop count, species count and unseen count — two convoys on the same day are otherwise indistinguishable.
Unseen birds are listed before seen ones, and 'nothing unseen here' is stated plainly: that is a direct answer to 'should I drive this route?'
limits: Names are never printed — open a checklist to see who. The species count is omitted rather than shown as 0 when detail has not loaded.

favResults.summary: Your own pinned hotspots, in your own order, each showing what is worth driving for right now.
inputs: the region's hotspot reference list, cached on device for a day
the last 7 days of reports at each pinned hotspot
the merged rarity snapshot the chase sections already fetched, so no extra notable call is made
how: Search matches on word starts across the hotspot name, requires every term to match, and ranks by all-time species count.
Order is yours: each pin has up/down controls and is never re-sorted behind your back.
Each pin lists only what would make you go: rarities (⭐), watchlist verifications (🔍), and species you have not logged this year — sorted in that order, newest first.
Common birds you have already seen are dropped on purpose: a hotspot's own species list answers 'what lives here', not 'should I drive there today'.
Your own checklists are excluded, so the list is what OTHERS are finding at your regular spots.
The header counts species seen in the last 7 days and reports filed in the last 24 hours, so a quiet spot reads as quiet rather than as a loading failure.
limits: Stored on this device only — pins do not sync.
One hotspot feed per pin, loaded serially when the section opens; reordering or deleting a pin repaints from cache rather than refetching.
A hotspot saved by coordinates rather than an eBird hotspot ID has no feed to read, and says so.

allUnseenBtn.summary: Every unseen bird you could go and see today, grouped by species, with each hotspot and its checklists beneath it.
inputs: all county and geo feeds
how: Bucketed by (species, DAY) first, then clustered to 250 m.
The day key is load-bearing: clustering without it merges Tuesday's bird into Saturday's pin and reports a stale sighting as current.

Places are then merged by HOTSPOT NAME, because eBird issues a separate location id for every personal location — one hotspot otherwise arrives as several rows with the same name, each holding one checklist.
Every checklist for a hotspot is kept and listed newest first, deduplicated by submission id.
Duplicate observers of the same bird, at the same spot, on the same day are merged into ONE row: six birders standing together at one stakeout is one place to drive to, not six leads.
The row shows the checklist time, the tally and how far away it is; a warning triangle marks a report eBird has not yet reviewed.
Filtered to the shared chase radius; places beyond it are collapsed into an expander rather than dropped.
The five most recent places show under each bird and the rest fold into a second expander, so one bird reported at 66 places does not bury the next species.
Species sorted nearest first, places within a species by date.
limits: Distance is straight-line, not drive time — a ferry or a lake can make a near place far.
Beyond the chase radius the list is still complete, just collapsed; it is not a claim that nothing is out there.

spLookupBtn.summary: Ask where ANY bird is being seen — including ones already on your year list.
inputs: eBird product/spplist for the region, to turn typed text into a species code
data/obs/{region}/recent/{code}, the per-species observation feed
how: Typed text is matched against common and scientific names; one hit goes straight to the birds rather than showing a menu of one.
Observations are grouped by location, keeping each place's most recent sighting and its highest count.
Sorted by date (most recent first) or by distance from home — the two different questions 'is it still around' and 'how far must I drive'.
Looks back 30 days, wider than the chase feeds, because a lookup is asked about birds that may not be present today.
limits: App-only: a Markdown report cannot take a query, and printing every species' places for a region would be a phone book, not a section.
Absence is an answer, not an error — no rows means it is not being reported right now, which is exactly what you asked.
Covers what eBird has for the region; a bird seen only outside it will not appear.

iconicBtn.summary: Which places near you are unusually good for one particular bird — the signal eBird's own hotspot pages call Iconic Birds.
inputs: eBird ref/hotspot/{region}, the cached hotspot directory, for places within your chase radius
GBIF occurrence facets over the eBird Observation Dataset — keyless, so this costs no eBird quota
GBIF geocode/reverse, to resolve each hotspot to the county it sits in
how: For each hotspot, ONE faceted GBIF call returns every species' share of the records in a 2 km box around it, together with the box total. A second call does the same for the whole county, and is shared by every hotspot inside it.

The multiplier is the bird's share of records at the place divided by its share across the county. Against eBird's own Iconic Birds panel at Mann Rd, Sultan this reproduces eBird's exact ordering: Yellow-breasted Chat, then Western Kingbird, then Lazuli Bunting, then Eastern Kingbird.

Measured across the WHOLE YEAR, not the current season. eBird's August-only view at Bolt Creek Burn omits the Northern House Wren the site is known for, because it is a May–June bird there; every row therefore states which months its records fall in.
Two views of one scan: by BIRD keeps a row per bird-and-place pairing, so the same bird can appear for several places; by PLACE ranks hotspots by their single best bird.
limits: App-only. The numbers are measured against YOUR home and YOUR chase radius, which a Markdown report generated hours earlier cannot ask for.

Two evidence floors, and both matter. A box with under 200 bird records has no norm to compare against, and a species with fewer than 10 records there cannot support a ratio — without the second, Bolt Creek Burn reports a House Wren at 82× off THREE records, which is the same artifact eBird itself prints as ‘130×, observed 1/1 years’.
Historical odds, not sightings. A high multiplier says the bird is reliably reported there, not that it is there today — there is no checklist behind a row.
Bounded to the 12 nearest hotspots and the top 4 birds at each, so a scan stays fast; GBIF's eBird snapshot also lags roughly a year, so very recent sites read thin.

easyBtn.summary: Common birds you should already have — the highest hit-rate chase list.
inputs: the accumulated history of daily report snapshots for this region
how: A species qualifies if it appeared on at least 40% of the sampled days and is not already on your year list, ranked by location-days: a bird reported from eight places is one you can go and get, while eight reports from one feeder is one lucky yard.

If fewer than 10 species clear that bar, the bar DROPS - 40%, then 25%, 15%, 8% - rather than print a two-row section. The intro always names the bar actually used, because '>=15% of days' is a materially different claim from '>=40%'.
Anything already on your year list is removed before the bar is applied, so widening can never resurrect a bird you have.
Ranked by how many different PLACES reported the bird, not by how many reports there were.
In the app the first run samples a month of checklists in the background; each day is cached, so every later run is instant.
limits: This section naturally shrinks as your year list grows, and that is correct: by mid-year you have already got the common birds. The widening ladder exists so a shrinking section degrades into a longer-shot list rather than into nothing.
A lower bar means a lower hit rate. A bird reported on 8% of days is a real target, but it is not the near-certainty a 40% bird is - read the stated threshold before driving.

The app and the report measure prevalence over different windows: the report uses every daily snapshot it has committed for the region, the app samples the last 30 days live, so the two can pick different bars on the same day.

nvResults.summary: Tentative IDs you still owe a confirmation sighting - and the one list that changes what counts as "seen".
inputs: birdlist-needsverification.md - a hand-maintained numbered list of common names
the same merged county + geo observation feeds every other chase section reads
how: Each name is resolved to an eBird species code against your birdlists first, then against the full eBird taxonomy, so a bird you have never recorded anywhere still resolves. A name that resolves to nothing is reported rather than dropped.

Those codes are SUBTRACTED from your seen set: seen = (year list + imported codes) - watchlist. That is why a watchlisted bird keeps appearing as a target in Closest spots, Easy misses and everywhere else - it is deliberately not counted as seen.

The section then shows the nearest report of each tracked species in the current window, closest first, with the checklist it came from. Species with no report in range are still listed, so the list is a complete inventory rather than only the ones that happen to be showing.
limits: The list is authored in the private pipeline repo. The app bundles it at build time and edits made in the app are stored on the device only - the app has no runtime GitHub dependency and cannot write the file back. Use the copy button and paste over birdlist-needsverification.md to make an edit stick in the Markdown report.
One list is shared by every region, because a tentative ID is tentative wherever you made it. A species you drop returns to your seen set only in reports whose year list actually contained it.
The species lookup searches birds recorded in the active region, so a bird never reported there will not appear in the picker.

migBtn.summary: What is arriving or leaving now, from multi-year history for these counties.
inputs: about two years of weekly historic observations, built up in the background
how: Species are compared against their own arrival and departure weeks in previous years to flag the ones due now.
limits: Needs the historic cache to be built; a fresh region has little to say until it fills.

bcBody.summary: Tonight's predicted migration intensity from BirdCast.
inputs: BirdCast forecast maps, per county
how: Links straight to the per-county radar forecast rather than re-hosting an interpretation of it.
limits: US only; BirdCast runs seasonally.

todBtn.summary: Birds most likely at the hour you are actually going out.
inputs: timestamps on the region's recent observations
how: Observations are bucketed by hour of day, and species whose reports concentrate in one bucket are called out as specialists for that window.
limits: Reflects when BIRDERS are out as much as when birds are active; dawn is over-represented in every dataset.

myYearBody.summary: Your year list for the region, exactly as the report prints it.
inputs: your eBird year-list export for this region
how: Oldest is numbered 1; newest is listed first. Each entry links its species page, its checklist, and its location.
limits: Pasted from an eBird export, so it is as current as the last export — it does not update itself.

settingsPanel.summary: App-only: API key, region, anchors, text size and seen list.
how: Everything here is stored on this device only.
Home and tide station are stored PER REPORT — chasing from Woodinville is meaningless on the Big Island.

You can add your own regions for trips. They live only in the app, because the Markdown report's regions are compiled into it, and a new one starts with an empty seen list — on a trip that is very nearly true.

helpBody.summary: What every other section reads, how it decides, and what it cannot tell you.
inputs: section-docs.json, bundled with the app - no network
how: Walks the Contents menu in the order the menu itself shows, grouped the same way.
Each entry renders the SAME notes as that section’s own ℹ️ button, through the same renderer, so the two cannot disagree.
Sections that do not apply to the current report are left out, exactly as they are left out of the menu.
limits: It describes how a section is CALCULATED, not what it is showing you today - open the section for that.
A section with no notes yet says so rather than inventing an explanation.

recordBody.summary: The megararities that are DUE here — rare enough to be a record, and not found yet this year. Scope it to your county for targets you might actually break.
inputs: a bundled list computed offline from GBIF, refreshed on app release
your region, and which scope you picked — the whole state, or one county
today's month, to rank by what is plausible NOW
how: Counts DISTINCT YEARS a species has been recorded here, never observations — one twitched bird inflates a row count 12-17x, so Terek Sandpiper's 15 Washington 'records' are one bird over two days.

Uses a 10-year window, because eBird's growth means an all-time count compares eras that are not comparable. Measured: this roughly triples the hit rate and halves the list. Washington's records committee reached the same rule independently — its review list is 'birds with 20 or fewer records in the previous 10-year period'.

Adds evidence from ecologically similar regions, which is the only way a bird with NO local history can be predicted at all. The Terek found at Stanwood in July 2026 had one prior precedent: Sooke, BC, the same fortnight in 1987.

At COUNTY scope the comparison region is the parent state, because a vagrant loose in Washington is loose in Washington. Measured: of the 132 species recorded in Washington but never in King County, the state reaches all 132 in one query while the three most similar counties reach 40.
Ranks by the odds for THIS MONTH, not by rarity. A 4% annual chance concentrated into one fortnight is a chase decision; spread across a year it is trivia.

Excludes escaped cagebirds by family, plus an explicit list of collection birds that families cannot express — Black Swan is a waterfowl, Golden Pheasant a phasianid, so excluding those families would delete Emperor Goose and Sooty Grouse with them.
The exclusions carry a per-region exemption, because countability is regional: Common Waxbill and Rose-ringed Parakeet are established and countable in Hawaii while being escapees on the mainland.
limits: It is a WATCHLIST, not a forecast. At state scope roughly one in six listed birds turns up within two years. A county record is a lower bar, which is why the county list is longer — no separate hit rate has been measured for it.
It cannot see a bird nobody has ever reported near you. A first record with no precedent anywhere in the region is exactly the case no history can predict.
Hawaii has no ecological peer in the ABA area, so its list can only contain birds already recorded there — a Hawaiian vagrant arrives off the Pacific, and no mainland state predicts it.
The list is bundled and only changes when the app updates, because the model needs decades of data the phone does not have. Only counties the reports cover are bundled.
A species rare next door because it is endangered and local, rather than because it wanders, can still slip in.
The escapee list is hand-authored, because no machine-readable source survived measurement — so a collection bird nobody has listed yet can still appear. African Collared-Dove does, for King County.

stakeHsBtn.summary: Everything about ONE place you have already chosen, rather than which place to choose.
inputs: eBird ref/hotspot/{region} for the name search, cached
eBird product/lists/{locId}, one call, which carries every recent checklist header AND its observer
how: The PATTERN leads, not today rows. How many checklists, across how many days, and what a visit is typically worth are true all day - unlike what was seen today, which is empty every morning by eBird own design.

MEASURED 2026-08-22 at 10:10: three target species returned ZERO reports from that day across the whole state. eBird embargoes checklists for an hour (its hotspot page says so) and people submit hours after the walk.

WHO BIRDS HERE is counted from the same single call, because product/lists carries userDisplayName. The patch-regular list is a different and more useful thing than the county top 100: the person to ask about a place is whoever actually birds it. Cedar River mouth reads Eric Hope 30.
Checklists are shown newest-first, which is the order product/lists returns - measured at three depths, 5, 50 and 200.
limits: It does not enumerate hidden checklists. Both species_recent and /data/obs/{loc}/recent/{code} collapse to ONE row per location - measured across 14 species at two hotspots, including owls, which was the sharpest test because owlers often use custom pins. Only /data/obs/{loc}/historic/{y}/{m}/{d} returns them all, at one call per DAY, and that cost is not spent here.
Checklist comments are not shown because they are in no eBird endpoint at all - hasComments measured true on ZERO of 2,860 rows.
